quote: Sir Roger Penrose—a world-class physicist—still thinks that consciousness is caused by quantum gravity. I expect that no one ever warned him against mysterious answers to mysterious questions—only told him his hypotheses needed to be falsifiable and have empirical consequences.
content: He was warned, at length and in public. Penrose’s argument is not from mystery but from Gödel, the Lucas–Penrose claim that human mathematicians can see truths no consistent formal system can prove, and the replies made the essay’s points in the essay’s terms: that the proposal “explains” consciousness by relocating it to a process no better understood (Grush and Churchland, “Gaps in Penrose’s Toilings,” Journal of Consciousness Studies, 1995); that the Gödel argument fails on its own logic (Putnam’s review in the New York Times Book Review, 1994; Feferman); and that the decoherence times make the mechanism physically impossible (Tegmark (2000)). Penrose has answered each and remained unpersuaded, which is a different failure from never having been told. The essay’s own annotation in Zombies! Zombies? praised Penrose for making a testable proposal and getting it tested; here the same conduct is evidence that the scientific tradition gives no warning against mysterious answers. The warning exists; Penrose heard it; he disagreed. That is what scientific disagreement looks like, and it is not evidence that the warning was never issued.

quote: In principle, all this could have been said in the immediate aftermath of vitalism. Just like elementary probability theory could have been invented by Archimedes, or the ancient Greeks could have theorized natural selection. But in fact no one ever warned me against any of these four dangers, in those terms
content: It was said, repeatedly, and it is on the syllabus. The first danger, an explanation that stops curiosity without controlling anticipation, is the virtus dormitiva joke in Molière’s Le Malade imaginaire (1673) and Peirce’s rule that nothing must “block the way of inquiry” (1899). The second, a hypothesis with no moving parts, is the mechanical philosophy’s demand from Boyle onward, and the criterion that an explanation must specify a mechanism is the subject of a large literature (Machamer, Darden and Craver, “Thinking about Mechanisms” (2000)). The fourth, an answer after which the phenomenon is as mysterious as before, is the requirement, in the deductive-nomological account, that an explanation show why the phenomenon was to be expected (Hempel & Oppenheim (1948)), and the whole of the post-Hempel literature on explanatory relevance. The third, cherishing one’s ignorance, is the obscurantism that Enlightenment writers attacked by name. These are not hidden; they are the first weeks of a philosophy of science course. The essay’s claim that “no standard warning exists” is true of the author’s own education and false of the tradition, and the essay generalizes from the first to the second.

quote: There is a known effect where great scientists have multiple great students. This may well be due to the mentors passing on skills that they can’t describe. But I don’t think that counts as part of standard science.
content: It is the standard mechanism, and it has been studied under its own name. Zuckerman’s Scientific Elite (1977) found that more than half of American Nobel laureates had trained under laureates, and attributed the effect to the transmission of tacit standards of problem choice and taste; Polanyi’s Personal Knowledge (1958) made tacit knowledge the centre of an account of science; Collins’s work on tacit knowledge in the laboratory, discussed in Book I’s annotations, documented that experimental skill cannot be transmitted by publication at all. The essay treats the fact that mentors cannot write down what they pass on as evidence that “these things are not well understood”; the sociology of science treats it as the reason apprenticeship exists. What the essay calls “standard science,” the published rules and the statistics courses, is the part of science that is written down because it can be; the part that makes scientists is the part the essay says does not count.

quote: Half of all the scientists out there still believe they believe in God! The more difficult skills are not standard!
content: About a third, on the surveys: 33% of the members of the American Association for the Advancement of Science reported belief in God and 18% in a higher power (Pew Research Center, 2009), and among academic scientists at research universities about a third believed in God with more or less doubt (Ecklund & Scheitle (2007)); half is the figure for religious identification, which includes the culturally affiliated. “Believe they believe” imports Book I’s belief-in-belief diagnosis as a description of a third of a profession, on the strength of a survey question that did not ask. The essay is entitled to the view that religious belief is a failure of rationality; the sentence as written misstates the number and reads minds in bulk.
